Did this MCMC fit converge?

Source: R/piml_bayesian.R
piml_bayes_converged.Rd

The single verdict function for piml_profile_fit_bayesian(). Every call site asks this rather than re-deriving the threshold rule – which is how the same inverted comparison came to sit in five places at once.

Usage

piml_bayes_converged(fit, rhat_max = 1.01, ess_min = 400, accept_min = 0.005)

Arguments

fit

An edaphos_piml_bayes object.

rhat_max

Numeric; the split-\(\hat{R}\) ceiling. Default 1.01.

ess_min

Numeric; the bulk-ESS floor. Default 400.

accept_min

Numeric; an acceptance rate below this is reported in its own right, because a frozen chain is easier to recognise from its acceptance rate than from a diagnostic. Default 0.005.

Value

A list with ok (logical, or NA when the object carries no MCMC diagnostics), reasons (character; empty when ok) and caveats (character; conditions that qualify the result without disqualifying it, such as an effective sample size that is an upper bound).

Why the comparison was inverted

Split-\(\hat{R}\) is undefined for a chain that never moved (Vehtari et al. 2021), and .piml_rhat_ess() correctly returned NA for it. But NA does not survive R's reductions in the direction a diagnostic needs: max(x, na.rm = TRUE) over an all-NA vector empties the argument set and returns \(-\infty\), the identity element of the maximum over an empty set; min likewise returns \(+\infty\). Both sit on the PASSING side of a one-sided threshold, so a chain with an acceptance rate of 0.00 was certified as converged. On a 60-profile sample of the shipped WoSIS extract, a quarter of every positive verdict was of that kind.

The diagnostics now encode an uncomputable statistic as \(\hat{R} = \infty\) and ESS \(= 0\), so every reduction fails on it, and this function reads them without na.rm.

References

Vehtari A, Gelman A, Simpson D, Carpenter B, Bürkner P-C (2021). Rank-normalization, folding, and localization: an improved \(\hat{R}\) for assessing convergence of MCMC. Bayesian Analysis 16:667-718.

See also

piml_profile_fit_bayesian()

Examples

# A frozen chain: R-hat is undefined, and the verdict says so rather than
# letting an empty-set reduction turn it into a pass.
frozen <- lapply(1:4, function(k) matrix(rep(k, 400), 200, 2))
dg <- edaphos:::.piml_rhat_ess(frozen)
dg$rhat          # Inf, not NA
#> [1] Inf Inf
max(dg$rhat, na.rm = TRUE) > 1.01   # TRUE -- this used to be FALSE
#> [1] TRUE
